name: Catalyst Arts
overview: Artist-run gallery at 6 Joys Entry in Belfast city centre, run by volunteers as a non-profit, members-based organisation: the committee is responsible to members, and directors serve limited terms (Catalyst Arts).

Founded in 1993 by MFA graduates of the Belfast School of Art as an artist-led project, led by joint co-directors who each served a two-year term. Nearly 100 people had held the role by 2018 (Catalyst Arts, "25 Years of Catalyst").
Wikipedia states it was founded to address what was seen as a lack of cultural activity and modelled on Transmission Gallery.
funding_verdict: Catalyst Arts: Arts Council of Northern Ireland and Belfast City Council, with Patreon members

name: The MAC
overview: Arts centre with galleries, theatres and a cafe bar at 10 Exchange Street West, in Belfast's Cathedral Quarter, opposite St Anne's Cathedral (MAC website; Wikipedia).

It is the successor to the Old Museum Arts Centre, which opened in 1989 and closed at the end of January 2010. The Metropolitan Arts Centre (the MAC) opened on 20 April 2012 (Wikipedia). It is a registered charity, NIC100808.

Building: designed by the Belfast firm Hackett Hall McKnight, completed in February 2012, with intersecting brick volumes and a basalt tower topped by glazing. It won a 2013 RIBA National Award and the 2014 Downes Medal (Wikipedia). The capital development cost £18m (Museums Association).
funding_verdict: The MAC: mainly public: Arts Council of Northern Ireland and Belfast City Council, plus foundations and trading income

press_items.title: unsigned news item, "Belfast's MAC seeks emergency funding" (20 December 2017)

name: Eastside Projects
overview: Artist-led gallery and commissioning organisation in Digbeth, Birmingham, at 86 Heath Mill Lane, B9 4AR. It describes itself as an "artist-led pluriverse" based in a free public gallery.

Founded in 2008 by six artists: Simon Bloor, Tom Bloor, Céline Condorelli, Ruth Claxton, James Langdon and Gavin Wade (Wikipedia). It opened on 26 September 2008 with the exhibition "This is the Gallery and the Gallery is Many Things". Current directors are Ruth Claxton and Gavin Wade (Wikipedia).
Birmingham City University says it set Eastside Projects up in 2008 and works with it in partnership. The gallery says it has worked with the university since 2008.
funding_verdict: Eastside Projects: Arts Council England National Portfolio, Birmingham City University partnership and trust support

name: Kettle's Yard
overview: The University of Cambridge's modern and contemporary art gallery: a house with a collection of 20th-century art and a gallery for exhibitions, on Castle Street, about a 30-minute walk from Cambridge main station (stated by Kettle's Yard).

Founded by Jim Ede and his wife Helen, who moved to Cambridge in 1956 and, with help from Winton Aldridge, converted four small cottages into one house for Ede's collection. Ede gave the house and collection to the University in 1966 (Wikipedia; Heritage Fund).

Building: a gallery by Leslie Martin was added in 1970. The site closed in June 2015 for a redevelopment that added a four-floor education wing, improved galleries, a new entrance and a cafe. Jamie Fobert Architects added a new courtyard, welcome area and shop. It reopened in February 2018. The interior of the house was left untouched (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Kettle's Yard: mainly public and university: the University of Cambridge and Arts Council England, plus earned income, trusts, individuals and corporate supporters

name: Pallant House Gallery
overview: Art gallery in a Grade I listed Queen Anne townhouse built in 1712 in Chichester, West Sussex, with a modern wing added in 2006 (Wikipedia).
Established in 1982. The house was council offices from 1919, restored in 1979, and has been run by an independent trust since 1985 (Wikipedia).
Named for the house itself, Pallant House. The collection began with works that Walter Hussey, Dean of Chichester Cathedral, left to Chichester in 1977 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Pallant House Gallery: mixed: charity income from visitors, Friends and patrons, with a district council grant and corporate partners

name: CCA Derry~Londonderry
overview: Contemporary art centre at 10-12 Artillery Street, Derry (Art Fund). Its Library/Workshop is also a Project Space visible from Artillery Street (CCA annual report to March 2024).
Traces its roots to 1992 as the Context Gallery, which developed in The Playhouse. It opened at Artillery Street in autumn 2012 in a building designed by Michael Carr Architects (Photoireland wiki).

Registered with the Charity Commission for Northern Ireland as the Centre for Contemporary Arts Derry-Londonderry, number 101414, since 10 February 2015. It had four employees in the year to 31 March 2025 (OpenCharities).
funding_verdict: CCA Derry~Londonderry: Arts Council of Northern Ireland as primary funder, with Derry City and Strabane District Council and project grants from trusts and charitable funds

name: Towner Eastbourne
overview: Public art gallery with a cinema in Devonshire Park, College Road, Eastbourne BN21 4JJ, beside the Congress Theatre (Towner website; Wikipedia).

Founded in 1920 through a bequest from Alderman John Chisholm Towner, who left 22 paintings and £6,000 for a gallery for the people of Eastbourne. It opened in 1923 in the Manor House in Old Town (Wikipedia).
Named for John Chisholm Towner (Wikipedia). Formerly the Towner Art Gallery.
funding_verdict: Towner Eastbourne: mainly public and grant-funded: Arts Council England and Eastbourne Borough Council, plus trusts, trading and the Newhaven Enterprise Zone

press_items.title: Gareth Harris, "Towner Art Gallery on England's south coast at risk as local council confirms funding cut" (2018)

name: Turn End
overview: Garden and three houses (Turn End, Middle Turn and The Turn) at Townside in the centre of Haddenham, Buckinghamshire, 3 miles north-east of Thame and 5 miles south-west of Aylesbury (the Trust's site).

The architect Peter Aldington designed the houses and built them with his wife Margaret between 1964 and 1968, including their own home Turn End. The Aldington family and founder trustees formed the Turn End Trust in 1998, and it became a charitable incorporated organisation in 2015 (the Trust's site, Find that Charity).
Named for its main house, Turn End.
funding_verdict: Turn End: small charity: Friends' subscriptions, events and local sponsors, in the founders' family home
wider_context: 20 July 2020: the Architects Climate Action Network wrote to Foster + Partners asking it to withdraw from designing a private airport terminal and control tower for the Amaala resort in Saudi Arabia or consider stepping down from Architects Declare, saying UK practices "should not be working to expand aviation" (Dezeen, Marcus Fairs, "ACAN calls on Foster + Partners to withdraw from Amaala airport project over climate concerns", 2020).

2 December 2020: Foster + Partners left Architects Declare over a disagreement about designing airports; Norman Foster said mobility is "the hallmark of our age" (Dezeen, Tom Ravenscroft, "Architects Declare 'disappointed' with Foster + Partners' decision to leave climate action group", 2020).

Both pieces concern the firm's design commissions, not Turn End, and neither names it. The link to Turn End: the Corporate Friends page thanks Foster and Partners for its support, with no amount stated.

name: The Hill House
overview: House museum on Upper Colquhoun Street in Helensburgh, on the Firth of Clyde, owned and run by the National Trust for Scotland, which acquired it in 1982. It has about 32,000 visitors a year (The Magazine Antiques, The Art Newspaper, Scottish Construction Now).

Charles Rennie Mackintosh designed it between 1902 and 1904 for the publisher Walter Blackie. Margaret Macdonald Mackintosh also designed interior elements, and English Wikipedia says the extent of her part is still debated.

A villa built of sandstone blocks under a Portland cement roughcast that let moisture in. The Trust removed the original roughcast in 2026 after five and a half months of work (Scottish Construction Now, The Art Newspaper).
funding_verdict: The Hill House: owned and funded by the National Trust for Scotland, with lottery and private money for the conservation project

press_items.title: Nancy Kenney, "Going undercover: Scotland's leaky Mackintosh treasure shielded by 197-tonne chainmail box" (2019)
no author named, "Application to keep Hill House 'box' until 2028" (2023)

name: Picker House
overview: House museum in a quiet cul-de-sac on Kingston Hill, run by the Stanley Picker Trust, whose guardians live on site (Trust).

Built for the arts patron Stanley Herbert Picker (1913 to 1982). The Trust says he set up the Trust in 1976, the Charity Commission registered it on 30 April 1976, and Kingston University's Stanley Picker Gallery dates it to 1977.
Named for Stanley Picker, who was born in New York, studied at Harvard and came to England to take over his father's cosmetics business (Stanley Picker Gallery).
funding_verdict: Picker House: endowed by its founder: a charitable trust funded from Stanley Picker's cosmetics fortune

name: Mostyn
overview: Contemporary gallery and visual arts centre at 12 Vaughan Street, Llandudno, North Wales, run by a registered charity (Mostyn Gallery Limited, charity 507842).

Its roots lie in the Gwynedd Ladies' Art Society, founded in 1894, whose first donor and founding member was Lady Augusta Mostyn. Wikipedia dates the original gallery 1901 to 1913, Andrew Graham-Dixon gives 1902. It was re-established as Oriel Mostyn and officially opened on 11 August 1979, and was renamed Mostyn after its 2010 refurbishment (Wikipedia).
Named for the Mostyn family, who built the original Edwardian gallery (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Mostyn: mainly public: Arts Council of Wales, with local councils, charitable trusts and shop income

press_items.title: Andrew Graham-Dixon, "The new Mostyn in Llandudno" (30 May 2010)

name: Auto Italia South East
overview: Artist-run gallery and commissioning organisation at 44 Bonner Road in Bethnal Green, London E2, in the London Borough of Tower Hamlets. Nearest Tube is Bethnal Green, nearest Overground is Cambridge Heath.

Founded in 2007 by Kate Cooper, Amanda Dennis and Rachel Pimm, who lived, worked and ran shows in a squatted car garage in Peckham, South London. It used donated buildings across the city for its first ten years (stated by the organisation). Wikipedia dates the Bonner Road space from 2016, after temporary spaces in Peckham (2007 to 2012) and Kings Cross (2013 to 2015).
Named for the garage, whose sign read "auto-italia south east" (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Auto Italia South East: grant-funded: public arts funding plus international cultural agencies, trusts and private giving

name: Cubitt
overview: Artist-run non-profit gallery, studio provider and education programme at 8 Angel Mews, Islington, London N1 9HH, in a former stables near Angel (Cubitt website; Islington Tribune).

Founded by artists in 1991 in King's Cross. It moved from Goods Way to Cubitt Street, which gave it its name, then to Caledonia Street, and later to Angel (Cubitt website; Wikipedia). Wikipedia does not name the founders.
Runs 32 artist studios, a non-profit gallery, an 18-month Curatorial Fellowship (the Curatorial Bursary from 2001 to 2015), a Civic Fellowship and Cubitt Community Radio (Cubitt website; Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Cubitt: public and charitable: Arts Council England support and donations; no studio rent figures published

name: Iniva (Institute of International Visual Arts)
overview: Visual arts organisation that runs exhibitions, commissions, residencies and the Stuart Hall Library, at Chelsea College of Arts, 16 John Islip Street, Pimlico (Chelsea College of Arts).
Founded in 1994 to address "an imbalance in the way culturally diverse artists and curators were being represented" in the UK. Stuart Hall was its first chair (Wikipedia, Chelsea College of Arts).
Was based at Rivington Place in Shoreditch, a five-floor building designed by David Adjaye that Iniva shared with Autograph ABP. It opened on 5 October 2007 and cost £5 million (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Iniva: Arts Council England National Portfolio Organisation, plus project grants from named funders

name: Isokon Gallery
overview: Micro-museum at the Isokon Flats, Lawn Road, London NW3 2XD, in the building's former garage (the gallery's site).

The gallery opened in 2014 and is run by The Isokon Gallery Trust, which Find that Charity records as registered as a charitable incorporated organisation on 26 March 2015. It is staffed by volunteers.
The gallery tells the story of the Isokon Flats, and Jack Pritchard created the Isokon furniture company in the early 1930s (the gallery's site).
funding_verdict: Isokon Gallery: volunteer-run charity: donations, shop sales and venue hire, with named business and individual supporters

name: Raven Row
overview: Non-profit contemporary art exhibition centre at 56 and 58 Artillery Lane, Spitalfields, near Liverpool Street station (Time Out; Wikipedia for the street address).

Founded by Alex Sainsbury, who bought the two houses in 2004 and opened the gallery in 2009 with a show by the New York artist Ray Johnson. Sainsbury set up a charity to run it (Wikipedia, Another Magazine).
Takes its name from the stretch of Artillery Lane that was called Raven Row until 1895 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Raven Row: self-funded: a private trust settled by its founder Alex Sainsbury

name: Sir John Soane's Museum
overview: House museum at 12 to 14 Lincoln's Inn Fields, Holborn, London, the former home of the architect John Soane (Wikipedia, annual report).

Established by the Sir John Soane's Museum Act 1833 (royal assent 20 April 1833), which took effect on Soane's death in 1837. Soane pursued the Act to disinherit his son George, with whom he had a long feud. The Act required the house and collections to be kept "as nearly as possible" as they were at his death (Wikipedia).

Named for its creator, John Soane, who bought No. 13 in 1806 and rebuilt it in 1808 to 1809 and 1812. No. 12 was connected in 1889 to 1890. No. 14, rebuilt by Soane in 1823 to 1824, was bought back by the trustees in 1997 with Heritage Lottery Fund help (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Sir John Soane's Museum: mixed: UK government grant-in-aid, trusts and individuals, and its own trading

press_items.title: Chris Foges, "An Exhibition at Sir John Soane's Museum Examines the Neoclassical Architect's Role as Modernist Forebear" (2025)

name: South London Gallery
overview: Contemporary art gallery on Peckham Road, south London, with a main site at 65 to 67 Peckham Road (galleries, bookshop, gardens, the café South London Louie) and the Fire Station galleries at 82 Peckham Road (South London Gallery).

Its origins lie in the South London Working Men's College, set up by the philanthropist William Rossiter in 1868 to "bring art to the people of South London" (South London Gallery). Wikipedia says the South London Fine Art Gallery opened on Peckham Road on 4 May 1891.

Wikipedia says the London Borough of Southwark took over responsibility for the gallery in 1965 under independent trustees, that David Thorp was appointed director in 1992 and that Margot Heller became director in 2001.
funding_verdict: South London Gallery: mixed public and private: Arts Council England and Southwark Council alongside foundations, Bloomberg Philanthropies support and patrons
wider_context: On 29 May 2026 more than 260 UK artists published an open letter asking five London theatres, the National Theatre, the Royal Shakespeare Company, the Young Vic, the Royal Court and the Almeida, to end partnerships with Bloomberg Philanthropies over its links to Israeli settlements (The New Arab).
Bloomberg Philanthropies is listed under "Ongoing Gallery Support" on the South London Gallery's current supporters page. The letter named no gallery.

name: Studio Voltaire
overview: Not-for-profit arts and education organisation at 1A Nelsons Row, Clapham, London SW4 7JR, championing emerging and under-represented artists. A registered charity and part of Arts Council England's National Portfolio (Studio Voltaire website).
Founded in 1994 by a group of artists and creatives in a disused tram shed. It moved to Nelsons Row in 1999 (Studio Voltaire website).

Building: the annexe was built in 1894 as a Mission Hall and Sunday School for Clapham Methodist church, and the gallery occupies the Victorian former mission hall (Studio Voltaire website). Wikipedia calls it a former Methodist chapel.
funding_verdict: Studio Voltaire: mixed: public funding (Arts Council England, Mayor of London), trusts and foundations, corporate patrons and individual supporters

name: The Showroom
overview: Not-for-profit contemporary art gallery at 63 Penfold Street, London NW8 8PQ, in Marylebone near Edgware Road (museum site; Wikipedia).

Established in 1983 at a site in Bethnal Green, East London (Wikipedia). It moved to Penfold Street in 2008 according to Wikipedia and in 2009, from Bonner Road, according to the Showroom's own history page.

Directors: David Thorp (1988 to 1992), Kim Sweet (1992 to 1998), Kirsty Ogg (1998 to 2008), Emily Pethick (2008 to 2018), Elvira Dyangani Ose (2018 to 2021). Gabriela Salgado was appointed in July 2022 (Showroom history page; Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: The Showroom: mainly public and trust-funded: Arts Council England, Paul Hamlyn Foundation and local London funders
